claim: The hierarchical surface structure with differential wettability creates capillary forces that actively pull droplets toward hydrophilic regions
mechanism: Microstructured hydrophilic regions generate stronger capillary forces than hydrophobic regions, creating a wettability gradient that drives directional transport of water droplets without requiring external energy input
evidence: Insect exoskeletons demonstrate directional water transport
Microstructured surfaces show enhanced droplet mobility
Wettability gradients have been shown to influence droplet movement
assumptions: Capillary forces are the primary driving mechanism
Wettability gradient is maintained during droplet transport
Surface tension differences are sufficient to overcome adhesion forces
expected_failure_modes: Capillary forces insufficient to overcome droplet adhesion
Gradient degradation over time due to surface contamination
Inconsistent transport under varying humidity conditions
novelty_rationale: This hypothesis specifically identifies capillary forces as the primary mechanism, distinguishing it from other potential driving forces
testability: Can be tested by measuring capillary forces at different wettability interfaces and correlating with droplet transport rates
falsifier: If droplets move toward hydrophobic regions instead of hydrophilic regions, or if transport occurs equally in both directions when wettability gradient is eliminated
